title: Orders of reaction and parameters from data

segs.text: Module one, objective four. Orders of reaction, and parameters from a data set. The rate of a process is the amount or concentration lost per unit of time. The order says whether that rate depends on how much drug is present: in zero order it does not, and in first order it does. The rate constant, k, is a fixed number, not the rate itself, and the half-life is the time for the level to fall by half. An I V bolus, a single dose injected into a vein all at once, is taken as first order; a data table has to be tested.

card.m: rate = {{frac:dC|dt}}: concentration lost per time, e.g. mg/L per hr
zero order: rate does not depend on C   first order: rate depends on C
k: rate constant, fixed; not the rate
t<sub>½</sub>: time to fall by half, e.g. hr
IV bolus → first order   data table → decide

segs.text: In a zero order process the same amount or concentration is lost every hour, however much drug is left. She said, It doesn't matter if we start at a thousand milligrams or if we start at ten milligrams, the rate of elimination is going to be constant. Because a fixed amount is lost from a shrinking level, the fraction lost each hour grows as the level falls. On linear axes the fall is a straight line, and its slope is the rate. A lower starting level halves sooner, because less has to be lost at the same rate, so the half-life is not constant.

card.m: zero order: same amount lost per hour
fixed amount per hour → the fraction lost grows as C falls
e.g. her table, 12 hr each: 206 → 134 mg/mL loses 72 (35%); 134 → 62 loses 72 (54%)
linear axes: straight line; slope = rate
t<sub>½</sub> shorter from a lower start
e.g. 6 (mg/mL)/hr: 350 → 175 takes 29.2 hr; 175 → 87.5 takes 14.6 hr

segs.text: In a first order process the same fraction is lost every hour, so more drug is lost per hour when more drug is present. The rate is fastest at the top of the curve, where the concentration is highest, and slows as the concentration falls. In her practice table, from twelve to twenty four hours and again from twenty four to thirty six hours, the earlier level divided by the later one was two point eight three, yet the loss fell from eighty to about twenty eight milligrams per liter. On linear axes this is a curve, and on a semilog axis it is a straight line. Halving is always the same fraction, so it always takes the same time: the half-life is constant.

card.m: first order: same fraction lost per hour
rate highest at the top, falls with C
linear axes: curve   semilog axis: straight line
t<sub>½</sub> constant: e.g. 350 → 175 and 175 → 87.5 mg/L both take 8 hr

segs.text: The rate and the rate constant are different quantities. For zero order, d C by d t equals minus k: the rate is k itself, with no C in it, so k is a rate, in concentration or amount per time. For first order, d C by d t equals minus k times C: k stays fixed while C falls, so the rate falls, and k is in reciprocal time, such as per hour. She said, If it's just K all by itself, it's independent of concentration. The minus sign shows only that the level is falling; k is never negative.

card.m: zero: {{frac:dC|dt}} = −k; k in (mg/mL)/hr or mg/hr
first: {{frac:dC|dt}} = −kC; k in hr<sup>−1</sup>
k C in the rate: depends on C   k alone: does not
k never negative; the minus sign = falling

segs.text: For first order, the half-life equals zero point six nine three over k. No concentration appears in it, so the half-life does not depend on concentration, and with k on the bottom a larger k gives a shorter half-life. She said, A constant divided by a constant is a constant. For zero order, the half-life equals C zero over two k, with the starting concentration, C zero, on the top, so a lower start gives a shorter half-life.

card.m: first: t<sub>½</sub> = {{frac:0.693|k}}
no C → t<sub>½</sub> constant; larger k → shorter t<sub>½</sub>
zero: t<sub>½</sub> = {{frac:C<sub>0</sub>|2k}}; lower C<sub>0</sub> → shorter t<sub>½</sub>

segs.text: Her practice set gives six concentrations over forty eight hours and asks for k, C zero, the half-life and the time to ninety percent decomposed. The order comes first: equal ratios over equal time spans mean a fixed fraction lost, first order, and equal differences per hour mean zero order. Here the earlier level divided by the later one is two point eight three from twelve to twenty four hours and again from twenty four to thirty six, so the table is first order. k comes from the natural log of C at two points, because the natural log of C falls along a straight line whose slope is minus k; the six and twenty four hour points give zero point zero eight six six per hour.

card.m: find k, C<sub>0</sub>, t<sub>½</sub>, time to 90% decomposed
equal ratios → first   equal differences per hr → zero
k = {{frac:ln C<sub>1</sub> − ln C<sub>2</sub>|t<sub>2</sub> − t<sub>1</sub>}}

segs.text: C zero is the twelve hour level times e to the plus k t; the exponent is positive because C zero must exceed every later level, and the result is three hundred fifty milligrams per liter. The half-life, zero point six nine three over k, is eight hours. For ninety percent decomposed, ten percent remains, so C zero cancels and the time is the natural log of ten over k, twenty six point six hours. When the percent remaining is a power of one half, she counts half-lives instead: with a half-life of eight hours, losing eighty seven point five percent of seven hundred fifty milligrams leaves one eighth, which takes three half-lives, twenty four hours, whatever the starting amount.

card.m: C<sub>0</sub> = C e<sup>+kt</sup>; kt = 0.0866 hr<sup>−1</sup> × 12 hr = 1.0392
C0 = 350 mg/L ✓ above 294.3
90% decomposed → 10% remains: C = 0.1 C<sub>0</sub>
87.5% lost = 3 t½ = 3 × 8 hr = 24 hr; the 750 mg is not used

segs.text: Her practice set also has a zero order table: from two to forty eight hours the level falls from three hundred thirty eight to sixty two milligrams per milliliter. From two to six hours the level falls by twenty four milligrams per milliliter, and from six to twelve hours by thirty six, both six milligrams per milliliter per hour, so the table is zero order. k is the fall in concentration over the time it took, six milligrams per milliliter per hour, and working back two hours adds twelve milligrams per milliliter to three hundred thirty eight, which gives C zero, three hundred fifty milligrams per milliliter. The half-life, C zero over two k, is twenty nine point two hours, and ninety percent decomposed takes fifty two point five hours.

card.m: 338 − 314 = 24 mg/mL in 4 hr   314 − 278 = 36 mg/mL in 6 hr
both 6 (mg/mL)/hr → zero order
k = {{frac:C1 − C2|t2 − t1}} = {{frac:338 − 206 mg/mL|24 hr − 2 hr}} = {{frac:132 mg/mL|22 hr}} → k = 6 (mg/mL)/hr
C0 = C + kt = 338 + 6 × 2 → C0 = 350 mg/mL

segs.text: Her Quiz one items match each order to its rate and its half-life. A rate that depends on concentration means first order: the half-life is independent of concentration, and d C by d t equals minus k C. A rate independent of concentration means zero order: the half-life depends on concentration, and d C by d t equals minus k. Her zero order item is keyed as a rate independent of the amount in the body; for first order she said, The rate is highest at the top of the curve when the concentration is highest. In her poll on first order, thirty eight percent chose the key, a constant half-life, and forty four percent chose units of k of concentration per time, which are zero order units.

card.m: rate depends on C → first order: t<sub>½</sub> independent ✓   {{frac:dC|dt}} = −kC ✓
rate independent of C → zero order: t<sub>½</sub> depends on C<sub>0</sub>   {{frac:dC|dt}} = −k
first: rate highest at the top   zero: rate independent of the amount
first order: constant t<sub>½</sub> ✓
✗ constant rate   ✗ {{frac:dC|dt}} = −k   ✗ k in concentration per time: all zero order

segs.text: An axis marked one, ten, one hundred, one thousand is a log scale even when it is not labelled, so a straight line on it means first order. She said, I expect you to give me half-life in units of time. Working back to C zero, the k t term carries a plus sign, because C zero is higher than every later level, and k is kept to three or four decimal places. Both orders return in Module eight: some drugs are eliminated by first order at drug levels well below a concentration called K M, and near zero order well above it.

card.m: 1, 10, 100, 1000 → log axis; straight line → first order
t<sub>½</sub> in hr or days, never hr<sup>−1</sup>
C<sub>0</sub>: plus sign   k: 3 to 4 decimals
Module 8: C<sub>p</sub> ≪ K<sub>M</sub> → first order   C<sub>p</sub> ≫ K<sub>M</sub> → near zero order
